translations.text: March 30. The life of the venerable father John, abbot of the holy mountain of Sinai.

Whose surname was Scholasticus. As for the city that gave birth to and brought up this valiant man before his monastic life, that wondrous city, so to speak, is an earthly one. I have no need to speak of it, but rather of the city that has now received him and feeds this wondrous man with nourishment that is not food,
I am not ignorant of it; rather, I know it very well. For he too is now in that city
of which Paul cries out with a loud voice, saying, “Their citizenship is in heaven.”

satisfying with immaterial nourishment one who cannot be satisfied, as he beholds the beauty of the invisible God, contemplating it with the understanding of his mind alone and marveling, having received gifts and crowns worthy of his labors,
having been numbered among those whose feet stand on the straight path, and remaining with them forever. How, then, he came there in a material body to stand among the [?] was plainly related.
The blessed man was sixteen years old in age, but a thousand years old in intellectual
skill, when he presented himself like a pure, freely offered sacrifice to the great High Priest,
He brought his body to Mount Sinai and his soul, I think, to the heavenly mountain, so that from that very place [?] toward the great but invisible [?].

Having resolved to gain guidance and progress, and living there, he took on great humility. He cut off all his own will from himself and bowed his neck in humility, and so of his own free will he put to death his impulse [?].
as though he had a soul without reason or a will of its own,

and had become completely changed from his natural disposition. What is still more remarkable is that, despite his great wisdom, he drove away pride in his wisdom through a simple life and humility. Then, after nineteen years, he sent his teacher ahead to the King on high, as a kind of envoy and intercessor.
he went out to a place of silence, carrying the abbot’s prayers in his hand like a weapon to strengthen himself.
He took up residence in a place five stadia away from the monastery. The name of that place was Tholas. He spent forty years living there,
without growing weary and with burning love,
and with divine
fire continually blazing within him.
And who is capable of recounting in words

Of his virtues and the labours he performed while living there, I will at least tell a little, from the beginnings of this blessed man's good resolve. He ate of everything, but very sparingly, for the sake of the commandment, not so that he might take pride in it but so that he might always keep his humility. He carefully kept himself from every kind of ointment [?]. At all hours

he meditated on death and so roused his soul to greater labours. Through obedience he cut off the tormentor's enmity as if with a sword. Through seclusion and silence he put to death vainglory, which is flimsier than a spider's web. How can I tell of the crowns he wove for himself in our presence with his streaming tears? Their secret work still remains [?] to this day in the cave, which stood a short distance from his cell.
There he would always sit weeping with tears, crying out and shouting loudly, as though someone had pierced his eyes with a weapon.

He took only enough sleep to keep from losing his mind through sleeplessness. Above all, before sleeping he would offer prayers and read books, for this alone brought him relief from despondency. His course was unceasing prayer,

and his love for God was beyond measure. For night and day, beholding God as in a mirror through the purity of his life, he could never have enough. A certain Moses, one of the monks there, wished to imitate his life and begged the abbot to have John receive him as his disciple.

The abbot pressed him, pleading with him, and he took him in, and he stayed with him. One day Father John ordered Moses to go to a certain place, dig a channel, divert the water, and bring it to water the vegetables. When he reached the appointed place, he diligently carried out his instructions. When the midday heat came, Moses lay down beneath a large rock and rested in sleep. But the Lord, who desires no harm for his servants, intervened beforehand, as he always does. For while the great-minded father was in his cell praying to God, he grew drowsy and slept a little.
And he saw someone in priestly splendor waking him, reproaching him for sleeping, and saying, “John, how can you sleep without a care,
while Moses is in great danger?” He immediately sprang up and prayed for his disciple.
Then, when he returned in the evening, he asked him, “Did anything bad happen to you?”
He replied, “A large rock nearly crushed me while I was resting beneath it at midday.”

if he had not suddenly called out to me, so that I woke and jumped away. But the truly humble father, without revealing anything he had seen, secretly praised the good God. He was also an example and a healer of invisible wounds, as once with a certain man named Isaac.
severely oppressed by the burden of a lustful demon and brought to despair, hurried to this wise father.

With tears and cries he confessed how the struggle had wounded him. The blessed man, marveling at his faith, said, “Let us stand in prayer, my friend.” And as the words of the prayer were coming to an end, while the suffering man was still lying face down,

the Lord, who fulfills the will of those who please him, heard his servant’s prayers and relieved that brother’s struggle. Both gave thanks to the Lord God. Some, goaded by envy, called him a chatterbox and a babbler. Teaching them through his actions, he showed everyone that he could do all things through Christ, who gave him strength in everything. He remained silent for an entire year, saying nothing to anyone, so that his detractors became petitioners, saying:
“The ever-flowing spring has been shut off, and everyone’s salvation has been lost.”

When they had prevailed upon him, he resumed his former way of life. Then, marveling at all his accomplishments, they all raised him to leadership over the brethren, as though he were a newly revealed Moses.
placing the lamp on the chief lampstand. These good judges had considered the matter, and they were not mistaken.
He too ascends the mountain and, passing through the impenetrable darkness, receives the God-fashioned law, being raised by spiritual steps; and [?] opens his mouth with the word of God.
draws in the Spirit, and pours forth a word and sayings, and good things from the treasury of his heart.

He reaches the end of his visible life while guiding the Israelite monks. In only one respect was he unlike Moses: he entered the heavenly Jerusalem, whereas Moses was somehow denied entry into the earthly one. Many bear witness to these things,
who have been saved and are being saved through him. The valiant new David is a witness to the wise man’s wisdom and salvation.
Our venerable pastor John is also a good witness. At his request, as a memorial, from Mount
This new seer of God came down to us from the Sinai of contemplation. He also showed us his tablets written by God, active on the outside and contemplative on the inside,
which carry confirmation, and say this:
Glory be to our God, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
